messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Default priors
parts:
Hmm, let me make some recommendations:

First, the general ladder of priors:
1. Noninformative
2. Weakly informative
3. Informative

A noninformative prior is typically uniform; it’s what we get when no prior is specified at all (which is why I’ve called it a “default default”).

A weakly informative prior will typically have a scale set to some value larger than 1, on the assumption that the data have been scaled so that parameters should not be much more than 1 in absolute value. Even after rescaling, though, parameters often _can_ be much less than 1, for example .01 or .001 or even closer to 0). For this reason, our weakly informative priors typically put a (soft) constraint on the parameter at the high end but not at the low end. This is why a weakly informative prior can often be specified using just one hyperparameter. This hyperparameter could have a default value of 10, but for some classes of models that we understand well, we might recommend a smaller value for the default scale, for example 2.5 for logistic regression coefficients.

An informative prior will typically have two hyperparameters, which can be conceptualized as a prior estimate and uncertainty, or as a lower and upper prior bound.

And there are various intermediate steps. For example, we can be moderately informative, using some subject-matter knowledge to (soft)-constrain a prior distribution but without trying to fully include all prior knowledge. This can make sense in settings where default weakly informative priors don’t regularize enough, but where we don’t want to put in the effort to fully quantify our prior information.

I’ve struggled for years to put all this in a theoretical framework, and I’m still struggling. Still, I think what I’m saying is reasonable.

Also, the side note that in some settings we might want boundary-avoiding priors for point estimation (for example, to keep hierarchical variance parameters away from 0) while in other settings we might be happy for point estimates to be on the boundary or to hit some special value (for example, in lasso regression where it is considered desirable to get coefficient estimates of 0).

There’s also this attached paper by Sander Greenland who recommends the log-F family of priors, which he says has better properties than the Cauchy which I’ve been recommending. He may well be right; I’d never thought that hard about the functional form but I agree that Cauchy is pretty extreme for most applications.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Default priors
parts:
For what it’s worth, I like to classify priors by the different criteria
used to chose them.

The “non informative” priors are all dependent on the chosen parameterization (one
of the reasons why we keep getting confused between the Stan default being uniform
on the constrained or uniform on the unconstrained scale). Essentially you’re choosing
a distinguished parameterization as somehow identifying the right sense of ignorance.

Weakly informative priors set a scale to the problem, identifying “small” and “big” but
being relatively ignorant beyond that. These are nice because they provide a means
of actually converting domain knowledge into mathematical constructions.

Informative priors, as Andrew notes, add structure beyond the choice of scale.

messages.subject: Re: Default priors
parts:
Linas:
For a scale parameter, uniform(0,infinity) is the default default and will often work just fine.  A default weakly informative prior would be something like Cauchy+(0,10), where Cauchy+ is the Cauchy defined on (0,infinity).  I’m assuming the variable is scaled so that values on the order of magnitude 1 will be reasonable.
